title: Monitoring Before Prometheus: Nagios, Zabbix, SNMP, and StatsD
intro: Prometheus and Grafana are recent. Many estates are still watched by older systems: Nagios and its descendants (Icinga) run checks that say OK, WARNING, or CRITICAL; Zabbix collects through its own agents; network gear speaks SNMP; and applications emit StatsD counters. The ideas carry over; the shapes differ. You're on a monitoring host.

steps.prompt: A Nagios check is a small program that prints a line and exits with a code. Run the HTTP check against web-1 for the path /health, warning above 1 second and critical above 3.
steps.fake_output: HTTP WARNING: HTTP/1.1 200 OK - 412 bytes in 1.904 second response time |time=1.904000s;1.000000;3.000000;0.000000 size=412B;;;0
steps.explanation: The page loads, slowly: WARNING. The part after '|' is performance data.
steps.why: The plugin contract is the whole system: exit 0 is OK, 1 WARNING, 2 CRITICAL, 3 UNKNOWN, plus one line of text. Any script that follows it is a check, which is why thousands exist and why Nagios-style checks are everywhere. They answer 'is this OK right now?' well and 'how has it changed?' badly; that second question is what time-series systems were built for.

steps.prompt: Before reloading Nagios after editing its configuration, verify it.
steps.fake_output:
Running pre-flight check on configuration data...
Checking services...
	Checked 412 services.
Checking hosts...
Warning: Host 'old-jenkins' has no services associated with it!
	Checked 41 hosts.

Total Warnings: 1
Total Errors:   0

Things look okay - No serious problems were detected during the pre-flight check
steps.explanation: Valid, with one warning: a host with nothing checked on it.
steps.why: The same test-before-reload discipline as nginx, Prometheus, and HAProxy. A Nagios configuration with an error stops the whole monitoring system on restart, and a monitoring system that's down is silent, which looks exactly like everything being fine.

steps.prompt: Switches, routers, printers, and UPS units report through SNMP. Walk the interface names of the switch sw-core-1 using SNMP v2c with the community string in $SNMP_COMMUNITY (the interface-description table is OID 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.2).
steps.fake_output:
IF-MIB::ifDescr.1 = STRING: GigabitEthernet1/0/1
IF-MIB::ifDescr.2 = STRING: GigabitEthernet1/0/2
IF-MIB::ifDescr.48 = STRING: TenGigabitEthernet1/1/1
IF-MIB::ifDescr.49 = STRING: Vlan10
steps.explanation: The switch's interfaces, each with an index used by the other tables (traffic, errors, status).
steps.why: SNMP organises everything in a tree of numbered identifiers, described by MIB files that give them names. It's the lingua franca of network hardware and isn't going away. Version 2c's 'community string' is a password sent in clear text, which is why v2c belongs on a management network only and SNMPv3, with authentication and encryption, is preferred. Prometheus reads SNMP through the snmp_exporter.

steps.prompt: Ask a Zabbix agent on db-1 for its one-minute load average directly.
steps.explanation: The agent answered with the load average.
steps.why: Zabbix polls agents for items, identified by keys like this one, stores them as time series, and evaluates triggers against them: it's a full monitoring system in one product, common in enterprises and among hosting providers. 'zabbix_get' tests one item by hand, the way 'curl /metrics' tests an exporter: the first step when a graph has gone empty.

steps.prompt: An application sends metrics in the StatsD protocol: plain text over UDP. Send one count of the metric shop.orders.placed to a StatsD agent on localhost port 8125.
steps.fake_output: (no output: UDP sends and doesn't wait for a reply)
steps.explanation: One increment sent; the agent aggregates and flushes totals every few seconds.
steps.why: StatsD's design is push, fire-and-forget over UDP: sending a metric can never slow or break the application, and if the agent is down the numbers simply vanish. '|c' is a counter, '|ms' a timing, '|g' a gauge. Datadog's agent speaks it (DogStatsD), and Prometheus's statsd_exporter translates it, which is how older applications keep working when the backend changes.
